nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American; the dialect poem, the standard English lyric and the short story
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and short-story writer; the first African-American poet to achieve national fame and the central black poet of the 1890s.
biography: Born in Dayton, Ohio, on 27 June 1872, the son of former slaves from Kentucky; he was the only black student at his Dayton high school, where he edited the school paper with Orville Wright, and worked as an elevator operator while publishing his first poems. Majors and Minors (1895) was praised by William Dean Howells, and Lyrics of Lowly Life (1896) made him famous; he toured England, worked at the Library of Congress, married Alice Moore in 1898, and died of tuberculosis in Dayton on 9 February 1906.
literary_profile: Dunbar wrote in two registers and the tension between them is the heart of his achievement: the dialect poems gave his white audience the plantation nostalgia it wanted, while the standard English poems and the novels speak in the voice of an educated black American who knows exactly what the dialect trade costs. His best work — 'We Wear the Mask', 'Sympathy', The Sport of the Gods — is among the most important American writing about race at the turn of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: Dialect verse in the plantation tradition, handled with real lyric skill; standard English lyrics of great technical finish; the mask and the double voice; short stories of black urban and rural life; the novel of the colour line.
intellectual_concerns: Race and the mask of accommodation; the legacy of slavery; the black artist and the market; love, loss and mortality; the city and the migration north; the cost of the dialect tradition to black self-representation.
historical_significance: Dunbar is the first African-American poet of national reputation and the central black writer of the 1890s: 'We Wear the Mask' is one of the most quoted American poems, his dialect verse permanently shaped the black literary tradition, and his double register made him the key figure in the debate over African-American representation that runs from Chesnutt to Du Bois.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Oak and Ivy (1893); Majors and Minors (1895); Lyrics of Lowly Life (1896); Folks from Dixie (1898); The Uncalled (1898); Lyrics of the Hearthside (1899); Poems of Cabin and Field (1899); The Love of Landry (1900); The Fanatics (1901); The Sport of the Gods (1902); Lyrics of Love and Laughter (1903); In Old Plantation Days (1903); The Heart of Happy Hollow (1904); Lyrics of Sunshine and Shadow (1905); Joggin' Erlong (1906); The Complete Poems of Paul Laurence Dunbar (1913).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the family novel, the sensational story and the children's book
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of Little Women and, in her anonymous thrillers, one of the boldest American writers of the 1860s.
biography: Born in Germantown, Pennsylvania, on 29 November 1832, the daughter of the Transcendentalist Amos Bronson Alcott; she grew up in Concord among Emerson, Thoreau and Hawthorne, and supported the family by sewing, teaching and writing. Hospital Sketches (1863) came from her service as a nurse in the Civil War, where she contracted typhoid; the anonymous sensation stories of the 1860s paid the bills, and Little Women (1868-69) made her rich and famous. She died in Boston on 6 March 1888.
literary_profile: Alcott wrote the American family novel as a woman's economic document: Little Women is a book about girls who must work, and its charm rests on the frankness with which it treats money, ambition and disappointment. Her anonymous thrillers — Behind a Mask, Pauline's Passion and Punishment — are among the most subversive American stories of the decade, and her children's books created the modern moral novel for girls without ever being merely pious.
stylistic_characteristics: Domestic realism with a strong narrative voice; dialogue that individualises the sisters; comic episode; the sentimental climax undercut by irony; in the thrillers, the femme fatale and the revenge plot borrowed from the sensation novel.
intellectual_concerns: Women's work and the economics of the family; female ambition and the choice of vocation; sisterhood and rivalry; the Civil War and nursing; the Transcendentalist household and its ideals; poverty and respectability.
historical_significance: Alcott is the central American writer of the family novel and the creator of the most beloved girls' book in American literature: Little Women has never been out of print, and the recovery of her sensation fiction has established her as a far more daring writer than her reputation as a children's author suggested.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Flower Fables (1854); Hospital Sketches (1863); Pauline's Passion and Punishment (1863, as A. M. Barnard); Behind a Mask; or, A Woman's Power (1866, as A. M. nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the industrial sketch and the social-problem novel
literary_identity: Novelist and journalist; the author of 'Life in the Iron-Mills', the founding text of American literary realism and of the American industrial novel.
biography: Born Rebecca Blaine Harding in Washington, Pennsylvania, on 24 June 1831; she was educated at the Washington Female Seminary and taught school, then moved to Wheeling, Virginia, where she observed the iron mills and wrote 'Life in the Iron-Mills' for the Atlantic Monthly in 1861. She married the journalist Lemen Clark Davis in 1863 and wrote over five hundred stories, essays and serial novels for the periodical press, while raising a family in Philadelphia. She died in Mount Kisco, New York, on 29 September 1910.
literary_profile: Davis wrote the industrial novel before Howells or Garland: 'Life in the Iron-Mills' is the first American work of fiction to treat industrial labour as a subject of high literary art, and its portrait of the Welsh puddler Hugh Wolfe and his hunger for beauty is one of the founding scenes of American realism. Her war journalism of 1862 and her later essays on women's work are equally important, and her best fiction unites documentary observation with a symbolic intensity then unknown in American writing.
stylistic_characteristics: Documentary detail of mill work and company housing; the symbolic image (the korl sculpture, the river, the fire); direct address to the reader; the narrator's moral urgency; dialect and immigrant speech; the short story as social argument.
intellectual_concerns: Industrial labour and the American working class; poverty, wages and the mill town; the artist born in the wrong class; women's work and the 'woman question'; the Civil War and the hospital; immigration and the Welsh, Irish and German workers.
historical_significance: Davis is the founding figure of American literary realism and of the American industrial novel: 'Life in the Iron-Mills' anticipated Howells, Garland and Dreiser by thirty years, and her recovery in the 1970s made her a central figure in the canon of American women's writing and of the literature of labour.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: 'Life in the Iron-Mills' (Atlantic Monthly, 1861); Margaret Howth: A Story of To-Day (1862); Waiting for the Verdict (1868); Dallas Galbraith (1868); John Andross (1874); A Law Unto Herself (1878); Natasha (1884); Doctor Warrick's Daughters (1896); Frances Waldeaux (1897); Bits of Gossip (memoir, 1904); Life in the Iron Mills and Other Stories (1985, collected).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the spiritualist novel, the woman's novel and the social story
literary_identity: Novelist, poet and feminist; the most popular American woman novelist of the 1870s and the author of The Gates Ajar.
biography: Born Mary Gray Phelps in Andover, Massachusetts, on 31 August 1844, the daughter of a professor of sacred rhetoric and the writer Elizabeth Wooster Stuart Phelps; she took her mother's name after her death in 1852. The Gates Ajar (1868) made her famous at twenty-four; she wrote over fifty books, campaigned for women's education and dress reform, and was a leading opponent of vivisection. She taught at Boston University from 1883 and died in Newton, Massachusetts, on 28 January 1911.
literary_profile: Phelps wrote the American novel of the afterlife and of women's work: The Gates Ajar is the book in which Victorian American grief is answered by a domestic heaven, and it was the most consoling novel of the post-war decade. Her later fiction — The Story of Avis, Doctor Zay — is among the first American writing about women's professional ambition and the conflict between marriage and vocation.
stylistic_characteristics: Domestic detail extended into the afterlife; the first-person letter narrative; sentiment controlled by irony; the professional woman's interior life; argument carried by dialogue; the reformist aside.
intellectual_concerns: Death, mourning and the afterlife; women's education and professional work; marriage versus vocation; vivisection and animal suffering; the Civil War and its bereaved; spiritualism and faith.
historical_significance: Phelps was the best-selling American woman novelist of the 1870s and a significant feminist thinker: The Gates Ajar shaped the American literature of mourning, The Story of Avis is a founding text of the American novel of the woman artist, and Doctor Zay is one of the first American novels with a woman physician as its heroine.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: The Gates Ajar (1868); Hedged In (1870); The Silent Partner (1871); What to Wear? (1873); Poetic Studies (1875); The Story of Avis (1877); An Old Maid's Paradise (1879); Doctor Zay (1882); Beyond the Gates (1883); Songs of the Silent World (1885); Jack the Fisherman (1887); The Gates Between (1887); Donald Marcy (1893); A Singular Life (1895); The Supply at Saint Agatha's (1896); Within the Gates (1901); Trixy (1904); The Whole Family (with Henry James et al., 1908).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American; the poem of reform, the novel of the colour line and the lecture
literary_identity: Poet, novelist, essayist and lecturer; the most important African-American woman writer of the nineteenth century and the first black woman to publish a novel in the United States.
biography: Born Frances Ellen Watkins in Baltimore on 24 September 1825, orphaned early and raised by an uncle who was a Methodist minister and abolitionist; she taught in Ohio and Pennsylvania, and in 1854 delivered her first antislavery lecture, becoming a paid agent of the Maine Anti-Slavery Society. She married Fenton Harper in 1860 and was widowed in 1864; she then worked for the freedpeople in the South, helped found the National Association of Colored Women, and died in Philadelphia on 22 February 1911.
literary_profile: Harper wrote the literature of black reform as poetry and fiction: her poems were recited at meetings and passed from hand to hand, and Iola Leroy (1892) is the first novel by an African-American woman, a story of passing, slavery and service that answers the plantation tradition and Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin at once. Her verse is direct, public and designed for the platform, and her prose records the interior life of a black woman of education and faith.
stylistic_characteristics: Ballad and hymn metres with a strong rhetorical beat; narrative verse of slavery and escape; the novel of the colour line with a didactic purpose; the lecture as literature; direct address and biblical allusion.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery, emancipation and the duty of the freedpeople; racial uplift and education; the position of black women; passing and the colour line; temperance and Christian duty; the American nation and its betrayal of its own ideals.
historical_significance: Harper is the founding mother of African-American women's writing and the first black woman to publish a novel in America: Iola Leroy and Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects are central texts of nineteenth-century black literature, and her career as a lecturer made her the most widely heard black woman of her generation.
major_influences: Frances Watkins's uncle, William J. Watkins
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects (1854); Moses: A Story of the Nile (1869); Poems (1871); Sketches of Southern Life (1872); The Martyr of Alabama and Other Poems (1895); Iola Leroy; or, Shadows Uplifted (1892); Atlanta Offering: Poems (1895); The Sparrow's Fall and Other Poems (1897); Idylls of the Bible (1901); Complete Poems of Frances E. nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American; the first African-American woman's novel
literary_identity: Novelist and seamstress; the author of Our Nig, the first novel published by an African-American woman in the United States.
biography: Born Harriet E. Adams in Milford, New Hampshire, in 1825, apparently the daughter of a free black man and a white woman; she was indentured as a servant to a farm family after her father's death and was cruelly treated, then worked as a seamstress. She married Thomas Wilson, a fugitive slave and lecturer, who abandoned her, and she wrote Our Nig (1859) to raise money for herself and her son, who died young. She died in Quincy, Massachusetts, in 1900.
literary_profile: Wilson wrote the first African-American woman's novel and the first American novel about the free black experience in the North: Our Nig is a fictional autobiography of a mixed-race indentured servant in a New Hampshire household, and it takes the form of a domestic sentimental novel in order to indict northern racism and the 'peculiar institution' of New England servitude. Its recovery in 1983 rewrote the chronology of African-American fiction.
stylistic_characteristics: First-person and third-person autobiographical narrative; the sentimental domestic mode turned into protest; documentary detail of indentured labour; ironic addresses to the reader; the appeal for patronage printed with the text.
intellectual_concerns: Northern racism and 'slavery's shadows'; indentured servitude and child labour; the mixed-race woman and her vulnerability; Christian hypocrisy; the economics of the free black woman; motherhood and loss.
historical_significance: Our Nig is the founding novel of African-American women's literature and the first African-American novel to be published in the United States by a woman: its recovery in 1983 by Henry Louis Gates Jr pushed back the chronology of African-American fiction and made Wilson a central figure in American literary history.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Our Nig; or, Sketches from the Life of a Free Black (1859); Poems and letters published in the local press (1850s).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American; the slave narrative, the travel narrative, the novel and the drama
literary_identity: Writer, historian, playwright and abolitionist; the first African-American novelist and the first African-American playwright.
biography: Born into slavery near Lexington, Kentucky, in 1814; he escaped in 1834, took the name of a Quaker helper, and worked as a steam-boat steward on Lake Erie, where he assisted other fugitives across to Canada. He lectured for the American Anti-Slavery Society from 1843, travelled to Britain in 1849 and stayed five years, and wrote the first African-American novel (Clotel, 1853), the first African-American travel book, and a pioneering history of black Americans. He settled in Boston and died there on 6 November 1884.
literary_profile: Brown wrote the whole range of African-American literature for the first time: the narrative, the travel book, the novel, the play and the history. Clotel is the first African-American novel, and it takes the story of Thomas Jefferson's black daughter as the vehicle for an indictment of the founding father and the slave system; his travel writing and his histories invented a black public prose in America.
stylistic_characteristics: First-person testimony with documentary documents; the multiple plot of separated slave families; the travel narrative with statistics and anecdote; the historical compilation; the melodramatic scene of sale and escape.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery and the hypocrisy of the American republic; the founding fathers and race; the black family destroyed by sale; the North and the fugitive; Britain and Europe as places of relative freedom; the history of black achievement.
historical_significance: Brown is the first African-American novelist, playwright and travel writer and one of the founders of black American literature: Clotel is the first novel by an African-American, The Escape the first play, and his histories the first substantial black historiography in the United States.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Narrative of William W. Brown, a Fugitive Slave (1847); The Anti-Slavery Harp (songbook, 1848); Three Years in Europe (1852); Clotel; or, The President's Daughter (1853); The Escape; or, A Leap for Freedom (play, 1858); The Black Man: His Antecedents, His Genius, and His Achievements (1863); The Negro in the American Rebellion (1867); The Rising Son (1874); My Southern Home (1880).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American; the feminist essay and the literature of black women's education
literary_identity: Educator, writer and activist; the author of A Voice from the South, the founding text of black feminist thought.
biography: Born Anna Julia Haywood in Raleigh, North Carolina, on 10 August 1858, the daughter of an enslaved woman and her master; she studied at St Augustine's Normal School, married the teacher George Cooper in 1877 and was widowed in 1879, then taught at Wilberforce and at the M Street High School in Washington, and took degrees at Oberlin. A Voice from the South appeared in 1892; she received her PhD from the Sorbonne in 1925 and spent her last years at Freetown, Sierra Leone, and in Washington, dying there on 27 February 1964.
literary_profile: Cooper wrote the founding text of black feminist thought: A Voice from the South argues that the progress of the race depends on the education and elevation of its women, and it does so with a breadth of reference — Goethe, Shakespeare, the church fathers, the women's movement — that refuses the condescension of the age. Her prose is formal, dense and rhetorically superb, and her argument that race and gender must be thought together is a century ahead of its time.
stylistic_characteristics: Formal essay with extensive quotation; the argument from history and from the Bible; irony and the polite rebuke; the platform address; the memoir and the educational report.
intellectual_concerns: Black women's education and the 'woman question'; race and gender together; the black church and its failure to support women; the South and the education of the freedpeople; literature and the cultivation of the black mind.
historical_significance: Cooper is the founding figure of black feminist thought and one of the most important African-American intellectuals of the century: A Voice from the South is the first book-length work of black feminist theory, and its argument that the black woman is the pivot of racial progress has shaped the whole later tradition.
major_influences: Anna Julia Haywood's mother, Hannah Stanley
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: A Voice from the South (1892); L'Attitude de la France à l'égard de l'esclavage (doctoral thesis, 1925); The Third Step (essay, 1892); Addresses and educational reports (1880s-1920s); The Voice of Anna Julia Cooper (1998, collected writings).
